HEARD:November17,
18,19,20,21, 2003; March 25,26;August 18, 2004

bovard J.:

[
1
]

The Defendants were charged on January 18, 1999 under s. 2 (1) (a)
(i) of the
Trespass To Property Act
(enter premises when entry prohibited)
and have pleaded not guilty.

The Facts

[
2
]

According to an Agreed Statement of Fact, which was filed and made
Exhibit 30, the Defendants are members or associates of a group called Toronto
Action for Social Change (TASC).  TASC is a Social Action Group, which claims
to promote Building Community Through Non-Violent Action.  (Capitals in the
original)

[
3
]

On October 1, 1998 the Defendants were part of a group that
demonstrated at Queen’s Park against welfare cuts, which they said led to the
deaths of homeless people.  About 15-20 placard and banner carrying persons
attended on that day.  In a symbolic gesture, a small amount of water-soluble
stage blood was poured on the front wall of the building.  As a result of their
actions on that day they were all served with trespass notices, which prohibit
entry on the premises of the Legislative Precinct (Legislative Building at
Queen’s Park and surrounding grounds).

[
4
]

On November 29, 1998 TASC sent an open letter to the Speaker of the
House requesting that the bans be lifted. The letter said that they would
openly defy the bans on January 18, 1999 if they were not lifted.

[
5
]

On January 18, 1999, at 11:35 a.m., the Defendants and approximately
40 others from their group marched on Queen’s Park and protested on the
driveway at the front steps of the building.  They stood in the driveway
directly in front of the steps leading to the south doors of the legislative
building.  The Defendants admit that they were within the area defined in
Order-in-Council 957/90, which defines the Legislative Precinct, but they deny
as a matter of law, that this area constituted part of the Legislative
Precinct.

[
6
]

They held signs and banners quoting from the
Charter of Rights
And Freedoms
and

Martin Luther King, and protesting provincial
government cutbacks.  They read from statements about freedom and the effects
of government cutbacks.  They were peaceful and [after their demonstration
finished] they dispersed.  The trespass prohibitions were still in effect at
this time.  No one was prevented from entering or exiting the building, and the
tone of the demonstration was peaceful.  Afterwards, Summonses were sent to the
Defendants [charging them under s. 2 (1) (a) (i) of the
Trespass To Property
Act
] (enter premises when entry prohibited).  (Portions in brackets and
parentheses Added)

The Parties

[
7
]

The parties to this case are:  The Defendants, the Crown, and the
Speaker of the Ontario Legislative Assembly. The Speaker was added on consent
as a party pursuant to an Application to the Court.  The Speaker’s
participation is circumscribed as follows:  The Speaker will enjoy the full
rights of a party, which includes calling evidence of any kind, cross-examining
witnesses, and a right of appeal where appropriate, but all of this only with
regard to the issue of parliamentary privilege as it applies to the Speaker and
with regard to the validity and /or effectiveness of the bans against the
Defendants under the
Trespass To Property Act
(Page 121,
lines
26-33; page
122,
lines
1-8, November 17, 2003 Transcript).

The Position of the Crown and
of The Speaker Of the Legislative Assembly

[
8
]

The Crown and the Speaker submit that the Speaker was acting within
the ambit of parliamentary privilege when he issued the trespass notices that
banned the Defendants from the legislative precinct.  Therefore, his actions
are not reviewable by the court.

[
9
]

In case I find that the Speaker was not exercising parliamentary
privilege when he issued the trespass notices, the Crown makes other arguments,
to which I will refer below, that address the Defendants’ submissions that the
notices infringed their rights under sections 2(b) and (c) of the
Charter of
Rights and Freedoms.

The Position of the Defendants

[
10
]

First, the Defendants submit that the
Speaker was not acting in the exercise of parliamentary privilege when he
issued the trespass notices, because the area outside the front of the
legislative building, where the Defendants were demonstrating, does not fall
within the Legislative Precinct over which the Speaker has authority.

[
11
]

Second, even if the Speaker was acting in
the exercise of parliamentary privilege, if the Court is used to enforce the
bans and a conviction is registered against the Defendants, it would
unjustifiably limit the exercise of their
Charter

rights under
sections
2(b)
[freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression…] and (c) [freedom of
peaceful assembly].

[
12
]

Third, even if the Speaker was acting in the
exercise of parliamentary privilege, by choosing to call upon the processes of
the court by invoking the provisions of the
Trespass to Property Act

against the Defendants, the Speaker lost the protection of parliamentary privilege.

[
13
]

According to the Defendants’ Notice of
Application and Constitutional Issue, they seek:

•

An Order under
s. 24 (1)
of the
Charter

or
section 52
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
that declares invalid the
trespass notices issued by the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario
on October 1, 1998, because they ban the Defendants from “the premises of the
Legislative Precinct”, which is an unjustifiable limitation on their rights
under
sections 2 (b)
, (c) of the
Charter.
[This was abandoned because
the Speaker lifted the bans against all of the Defendants on August 16, 2004.]

•

A reading down of section 2 of the
Trespass
to Property Act (
R.S.C. 1990, chap. T.21) so that it does not apply to the
conduct of the Defendants in this case and to thereby render it consistent with
the Defendants’ rights under
sections 2 (b)
, (c) of the
Charter
.

•

An Order staying the proceedings because they
are an unjustifiable limitation on their rights under
sections 2 (b)
, (c) of
the
Charter
.

•

Costs

Disposition

[
14
]

I made findings
through out the judgment, but for the sake of convenience, I will list them all
together here. After considering all of the evidence, the relevant law, and the
submissions made by the parties I find that:

(1)

The
parliamentary privilege that is invoked in the case before me is the “ejection
of strangers from the House and its precincts.”

(2)

It is necessary
for the dignified and proper functioning of the Legislature of Ontario that the
Speaker have control over the grounds surrounding the Legislative building, and
for the Legislative Precinct to be defined so as to cover this area.

(3)

This control
comes within, and forms part of, the Speaker’s parliamentary privilege of the
“ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts”, because it is
necessary in order to ensure that nothing that occurs within    the Legislative
Precinct impedes the proper functioning of the  Legislative Assembly.

(4)

The Legislative
Precinct for the Legislature of Ontario is as it is defined in Order-in-Council
957/90 as being “…the entire Legislative building, the grounds bounded on the
east by Queen’s Park Crescent East, on the north by Wellesley Street West and
on the west by Queen’s Park Crescent West, and the first and second floors of
the Whitney Block;”

•

And in addition,
covers the added areas that the Speaker confirmed in a Memorandum of
Understanding between the Ministry of Government Of [sic] Services and The Office
of the Assembly, which was revised on October 15, 1992.  At paragraph 2.1 of
said Memorandum, “the tunnel connecting the Legislative building to the Whitney
Block; and the third floor and part of the basement of the Whitney Block “ were
added.  (See Exhibit I, Tab D, Affidavit of Mr. Desrosiers)

(5)

This was the
area in which the Defendants were demonstrating when the
Trespass to
Property Act
bans were issued to them, and the area to which the bans refer.

(6)

The exterior
wall of the Legislative building is a part of the building, and therefore, even
taking the definition of the precinct urged on me by the defence, it is within
the precinct, and the Defendants went into it when they poured the stage blood
on the building.

(7)

The reasons that
the bans were issued to the Defendants were:

•

Inspector Beale
asked the group with which the Defendants were demonstrating to leave several
times and they did not;

•

It was believed by
the Legislative Security Services that they defaced the Legislative building
with the blood-like substance;

•

The area of the
Legislature where the demonstration was taking place was not accessible from
that side.

(8)

The Speaker was
acting within the bounds of the recognized category of parliamentary privilege
of the “ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts” when he issued
the bans.

(9)

Given that the
parliamentary privilege in the case before me is necessary to the proper
functioning of the Legislature of Ontario, and that the reasons for which the
bans were issued fall within the privilege, I do not have the jurisdiction to
review the actions of the Speaker in any manner, including under the
Charter
of Rights And Freedoms.

(10)

Given the
findings that I made above, it is not necessary to address the Applicant’s
submissions that I should invoke the
Charter of Rights And Freedoms
to
read down the
Trespass to Property Act
so that it is consistent with
ss.
2 (b)
and (c) of the
Charter
,
or that I stay the proceedings on the
basis that they are an unjustifiable limitations of their rights under these sections.

(11)

Also, all
parties agree that since the bans against all of the Defendants are now lifted,
I do not have to adjudicate on the issue of a declaration of invalidity of the
bans as an unjustifiable limitation of their rights under these sections, because
it is a moot point.

(12)

Based on the
above reasons, I find that the Crown proved the charges against all of the
Defendants beyond a reasonable doubt, in that the evidence is uncontested that
on January 18, 1999 they entered an area from which they were banned. They are
all found guilty as charged, of entering premises when entry prohibited, to
wit:  Queen’s Park on January 18, 1999.

(13)

Finally, the
Defendants’ application for costs is dismissed.

The
Evidence

[
15
]

Claude Desrosiers, the Clerk of The
Legislative Assembly, testified.  He adopted what he said in his Affidavit (Exhibit
1), which he swore on November 4, 2003.  In addition, he said that he has been
the Clerk of The Legislative Assembly since 1986.  His training involved
working at the House of Commons in Ottawa.

[
16
]

He has two main duties:  (1) To offer
procedural advice to the Speaker and to the Members of the House while it is
sitting.  This involves how to pass legislation, how to debate, and how to
address issues before the House and its Committees.   (2) He is the chief
administrative officer under the Speaker and is responsible for everything that
is required for the Members to perform their functions.  He reports to the
Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and to the House.

[
17
]

In his capacity as Clerk of The Legislative
Assembly he is intimately familiar with the role of the Speaker.  He said that
the Speaker is the representative of the Members of the House, who elect him,
or her, and the Speaker is accountable to them.  His main role is to keep order
in the House and to make sure that the business of the House is accomplished in
the best manner.  He is responsible for Parliamentary procedure and for the
administration of the Legislature. He is the chairperson of the Board of
Internal Economy, which decides questions of budget and policy for the proper operation
of the House.

[
18
]

Regarding parliamentary privilege, he
described it as a set of rules, which evolved over centuries that are essential
to permit the Legislative Assembly to perform its functions.  He said that the
Legislatures themselves are the guardians of their own privileges.

[
19
]

Whenever parliamentary privilege is an issue
in court the Speaker seeks status as a party to the proceedings in order to
protect this privilege.  When the Speaker intervenes, the Attorney General does
not represent the Speaker, because the Attorney General is part of the
executive branch of government and the Speaker represents the legislative
branch.

[
20
]

The purpose of parliamentary privilege is to
allow the Members to perform their legislative functions freely, and to protect
the Legislative Assembly.

[
21
]

Mr. Desrosiers said that the Speaker’s power
to exclude non-Members from parts of the Legislative Precinct, other than the
Chamber of the House, derives from parliamentary privilege and the right of the
Speaker to administer the Legislative Building and to regulate its use and the
use of the grounds.

[
22
]

The power to regulate the use of the
Legislative Precinct derives from  “…long standing principles that the House
has devolved through the Speaker – the right to ensure that they have access.”
(Page 58, Lines 25-30, Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
23
]

He said that the Speaker draws his authority
from the Members of the House.  This is addressed in the
Legislative
Assembly Act
and in the internal rules passed by the Members in the
Standing Orders of the House, and by precedent.  He testified, at page 64,
lines 5-10, of the transcript of November 17, 2003, that s. 103(2) of the Legislative
Assembly Act is the basis of the authority for Memoranda of Understanding,
which, “…definitely go to giving control to the Speaker of the grounds.”  The
Memoranda to which he is referring are at Tab B of his Affidavit, which is
Exhibit 1, modified by the one at Tab D, and the one at Tab E.  (See page 60,
line 14; page 61, lines 7-17; page 62, lines 10-17; and page 64, lines 5-10)

[
24
]

However, Mr. Desrosiers stated emphatically
that the
definition
of the Legislative Precinct does not depend on the
Memoranda of Understanding.  The Legislative Assembly itself created the definition.
He said that he did not know the origins of the definition, but it did not
appear in written form prior to the Memoranda of Understanding being written.
But the Memoranda deal just with administrative matters and upkeep of the building
and the grounds, which up to the signing of the Memoranda was the
responsibility of a Ministry of the Government.  The definition of the
Legislative Precinct appears in the Memoranda just to help define the area for
which the Speaker will be responsible administratively vis-à-vis the
Government. The Memorandum dated August 29, 1988 has the effect of an Order-in-Council.

[
25
]

He described the Legislative Precinct as,
“…that geographical area which…surrounds the Parliament and can vary from Parliament
to Parliament depending on the individual geography that is attached to the
various Parliament, but it is usually that immediate area that surrounds the
Parliament and that can be said to be that area that Members need in order to
feel the freedom to do the job that they have to do. “ (Page 20, lines 17-24,
Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
26
]

The precise definition is contained in a
Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Government Services and the
Office of the Assembly (Exhibit 1, Tab B).  The Minister of Government Services
and the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly signed this Memorandum on August
29, 1988.  This description is also contained in Order-in-Council 957/90, dated
April 20, 1990. (Exhibit 1, Tab C).  The Order-in-Council was made pursuant to
The
Legislative Assembly Act
and
The Ministry of Government Services Act.

This was done to “…reinforce the idea that the Speaker was, indeed, responsible
for these areas.”  (Page 50, lines 12-15, Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
27
]

The Memorandum at Tab D describes the
Legislative Precinct as follows:  “…the entire Legislative Building, the
grounds bounded on the east by Queen’s Park Crescent East, on the north by
Wellesley Street West and on the west by Queen’s Park Crescent West, and the
first and second floors of the Whitney Block
;”
Mr. Desrosiers explained
that the southern boundary is not described because the east and west sides of
Queen’s Park Circle meet south of the Legislative building and that there was
no need to describe it.  The southerly completion of Queen’s Park Circle forms
the southern boundary.

[
28
]

Mr. Desrosiers added that three storeys of
the Whitney building, plus part of the basement of the Whitney building and the
tunnel that runs underneath Queen’s Park Circle east and that links the two
buildings are also part of the Legislative Precinct, but they are not relevant
to this case.  A map of the Legislative Precinct was made exhibit 2.  He said
that the tunnel is part of the Legislative Precinct because it is a necessary
link between the Whitney Block and the Legislative building.

[
29
]

He said that the grounds immediately
surrounding the Legislative building are included in the Legislative Precinct
because it is required in order to ensure access and egress to the Legislative
building.  Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that the demonstrations that
are permitted in front of the building be peaceful and do not prevent access
and egress of the Members of the Legislative Assembly to the Legislative
building.  Obviously, if they cannot get into the building they cannot perform
their functions.

[
30
]

He described how, in Ottawa, and at
Westminster in London, the area of the Legislative Precinct has evolved over
the years to accommodate more members.  More office space has been provided for
them, which office space is included in the Legislative Precinct.

[
31
]

He disagreed with J.P. Maingot’s comments
in, Parliamentary
Privilege in Canada, Second Edition
, regarding what
constitutes the Legislative Precinct of the House of Commons in Ottawa.  At
page 164 of his text, Mr. Maingot states that, “ It will be seen that the
grounds of Parliament Hill are not part of the [Legislative] precincts.”  Mr.
Desrosiers said that authorities are not always perfect and that they differ on
this point.  He pointed out that he does not believe that the Speaker in Ottawa
enjoys the benefit of the transfer of administrative responsibilities for the
Legislative building and the grounds that the Speaker does in Toronto.  In
Ottawa, Public Works (Canada) and the National Capital Commission still have a
lot of involvement with the administration of the building and the grounds.
These functions are not in the Speaker’s domain as they are in Toronto.

[
32
]

He said that Tab B of his Affidavit (Exhibit
1) is a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Government Services
and the Office of the Legislative Assembly that describes the administrative
division of powers between them.  For example, who is responsible for the
administration of the Legislative Precinct.  Tab C is an amendment to this
Memorandum.  It supplies more precision and complements the definition of the
Legislative Precinct. Tab D is another Memorandum of Understanding between the
Ministry of Government Services and the Speaker on behalf of the Legislative Assembly.
The purpose of this Memorandum was to ensure that “the provisions of the
service arrangements as dealt with by the two ministries involved were quite
well defined and well documented.”  (Page 21, lines 13-18, Transcript of
November 17, 2003)

[
33
]

According to him, the Memoranda of
Understanding referred to above are not necessary for the Speaker to control
access in the areas about which he has been speaking.  He said that making sure
that access to the Legislative Precinct is provided for the Members comes under
the Speaker’s parliamentary privilege.  The Memoranda are administrative in
nature.

[
34
]

Prior to their existence, the responsibility
for maintaining the Legislative building was on the Executive through the
Ministry of Public Works.  The Ontario Provincial Police and the Ontario
Government Protective Service, the agencies that provided security, reported to
the Executive.  The Memoranda were devised in order to ensure that “ the
Legislature under the Speaker and the staff of the Legislature would be the
ones that are responsible, as much as can be, for the maintenance of the
building and for the administration of the building.”  (Page 26, lines7-10,
Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
35
]

He said that as a result of the Memoranda,
the Legislative arm, through the Speaker, has the responsibility for
ninety-nine percent of what happens in the Legislature as far as administration
goes.

[
36
]

He explained that the Memoranda do not
mention security because it was taken for granted up to the point of the
signing of the Memoranda.  Security at the Parliament buildings was not an
issue until the late 1980s and the early 1990s.  Now the primary responsibility
for the administration of the law outside of the Legislative building has been
allocated to the Toronto Police Service pursuant to a Memorandum of
Understanding between the Speaker and the Metropolitan Toronto Police Service.
(Exhibit 1,Tab E)

[
37
]

Mr. Desrosiers mentioned several security
incidents that occurred since the early nineties, which in part motivated the
Speaker to ask the Standing Committee of the Legislative Assembly to report on
the matter of security for the Legislative Assembly.

[
38
]

In 1992 a group of persons came into the
Legislative building, first as individuals, and then re-grouped once inside.
They were outside of the Legislative Chamber. There were four or five members
of the Ontario Government Protective Service there, but there was nothing that
they could have done had the situation worsened.  A Member of the Legislature
who knew about the demonstration came out of his office and defused the
situation and convinced them to leave.  Mr. Desrosiers said that the
demonstration could have had “tragic consequences” and could have interrupted
the work of the Legislature.

[
39
]

Another group of persons barged into the
front door of the Legislative building and caused quite a bit of damage and
occupied the building for a period of time.

[
40
]

In 1996 the Legislative building was
surrounded during a strike of the public service workers.  He and the
Sergeant-at-Arms forced their way out of the building and went to court to get
an injunction simply to stop the demonstrators from preventing access and
egress to the Legislative building by the Members, not to stop them from
demonstrating.

[
41
]

The most dangerous situation occurred in
1995 on the day of the Opening of the Legislature.  He said that there were
many persons there to celebrate the Opening, such as, young pages, dignitaries,
and many other citizens.  However, the building was almost completely inundated
with persons as a result of a demonstration and it created a very dangerous
situation.

[
42
]

In 2000 there was a major incident,
described as a near riot, on the grounds of the Legislative building that was
handled by the police.  There have been other more minor incidents as well. He
said that Toronto Action for Social Change was not involved in any of these
disruptions.

[
43
]

Ms. Beagan Flood, counsel for the Speaker,
showed Mr. Desrosiers the
Report on Security in the Legislative Precincts
,
authored by the Standing Committee of the Legislative Assembly. This was made
Exhibit 3.   He said that after the Opening Day incident in 1995, the then
Speaker, Mr. McLean, on orders from the House, asked the Committee to investigate
the security issue at the Legislative Assembly in order to elaborate recommendations
to help the Speaker implement security measures.  The reason for this was that
the occurrence of dangerous situations at the Legislative building was escalating.
The incident on the day of the Opening of the Legislature in 1995 was the main
impetus for this action.  The Speaker thought that it was very important for
the Committee to examine how security was organized at the Legislative
Assembly.  Mr. Desrosiers testified that the Committee wrote the Report and
the
House adopted it.

[
44
]

As a result of the Committee’s Report, a
“stand alone security system” was put in place whereby employees of the
Legislature report to the Speaker through the Sergeant-at-Arms, who is in
charge of security for the Speaker. The “stand alone security system” would be
in charge of security inside of the Legislative building.

[
45
]

This model permits access to the Members
under the control of the Speaker.  The Committee recommended that another
Memorandum of Understanding (Exhibit 1, Tab B) be entered into by the Speaker
and the Metropolitan Toronto Police Services, which would provide for looking
after the outside of the Legislative building when a demonstration that would
put the building in danger was expected to occur.   These Memoranda of
Understanding were created by the Speaker
in response to a direct Order of
the House.

[
46
]

He testified that the Speaker does not need
the approval of the Executive with regard to the exercise of his protective
duties, and indeed it would be improper for there to be any such requirement.
The form letter (Exhibit 1, Tab K, last page), which the Defendants received
banning them from the Legislative Precinct was made on the authority of the
Speaker.

[
47
]

Mr. Desrosiers said
that if the Speaker does not have control over the grounds outside of the
Legislative building “…the legislature would be at the mercy of, not only a
dangerous situation, but also of a time consuming situation which could put in
jeopardy the work that it has to do.”  He said that, “…it is necessary that the
Speaker have control over the grounds in order to make sure – to ensure that
Members have access to and that nothing happens on the grounds that is
disruptive to the business of the Legislature.”  (Page 39, lines 8-23,
Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
48
]

He said further, at page 52, lines 20-28, of
the same transcript, that if the Speaker did not have control over the grounds
in the sense that he could not ban persons it would have immense
repercussions.  He would not be able to prevent anyone from doing what he or
she wanted on the grounds.  Anyone would be free to do anything that could be
interpreted as a demonstration and it could detrimentally affect the operation
of the Legislature.   It could also be detrimental because the Legislature
would have to spend an inordinate amount of time to control situations that got
out of hand.

[
49
]

In cross-examination, he said that if the
Speaker did not have this power, the police would still have the power to
administer the general law of the province and of Canada outside of the
Legislative building.  But he said that this authority would be exercised only
with the permission of the Speaker. He also said that the Courts would still be
able to exercise their civil jurisdiction over the grounds, as they did when
they granted the injunction to prohibit the demonstrators from preventing
access and egress to the Legislative building.

[
50
]

Mr. Desrosiers said that pursuant to s. 103
(2) of The
Legislative Assembly Act,
(Exhibit 1,Tab F)

the
Speaker established guidelines for security of the Chamber of the Legislature
and the parts of the Legislative building that are under his control. Tab G
contains the guidelines that he established. These guidelines are general rules
for the security unit at the Legislative Assembly on how to exercise their
functions.  They were in effect on January 18, 1999 (the date of the alleged
offences).  The policy at Tab I of Exhibit 1 is the one that was in force on
January 18, 1999.
(1)

[
51
]

Regarding the Legislative Security Services
(LSS), he said that persons who are planning a demonstration are encouraged to
contact them to tell them of their plans.  This is the recommended procedure.
Then LSS provides them with assistance. For example, they supply microphones
and other things for their demonstration.  The LSS also advises them of  “the
dos and don’ts of what a demonstration should do…”  (Page 40, lines 4-5,
Transcript of November 17, 2003)

[
52
]

Exhibit 1, Tab H is a
Bookings Manual for
The Legislative Assembly of Ontario, Policies and Procedures.
It explains
what persons have to do if they want to use the Legislature or the grounds for
any type of activity, including demonstrations.  The Executive does not play
any part in deciding whose applications are accepted or rejected.  This is
handled by a branch of the Legislature that works under the direction of the
Sergeant-at-Arms.  He emphasized that the Executive does not have anything to
do with how the Legislature goes about its business.

(1) Ms.
Beagan Flood, Counsel for the Speaker, discovered after all the evidence was in
that new Guidelines for demonstrations and special events on the Legislative
Building grounds were passed in January, 2004.  They were made Exhibit 31 on
consent.  The key changes are: (a) That if permission is granted to demonstrate
it does not mean that the Legislative Assembly endorses the organization or
what it says, and such endorsement may not be stated or implied in any public
announcement by the group, (b) A letter of support from a Member of Parliament
is no longer required, (c) There is no longer a prohibition against the
defacement of flags, (d) The material that the group plans to distribute no
longer has to be submitted beforehand, (e) The demonstration planned must be
consistent with others’ use of the grounds,  and (f)  illegal signs or speeches
of obscenity or hate are specifically prohibited.

[
53
]

If a group that did not make an application
shows up to demonstrate they can still perform their demonstration. The only
thing that happens as a result of not applying is that the Legislature does not
provide them with microphones and various other things to help them
demonstrate, which they provide to persons who do apply.  If a group of demonstrators
causes a danger that they cannot deal with, they call the Metropolitan Toronto
Police.  He believed that it is the police that make the decision to arrest
someone at a demonstration.   The Speaker has nothing to do with that
decision.  When the Speaker’s guidelines are breached outside of the Parliament
Building, the police deal with the suspects, not the Speaker.

[

Analysis

What
is the type of parliamentary privilege that is invoked in the case before me?

[
141
]

In
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v.
Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly)
,
1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
,
[1993] 1 S.C.R. 319

at paragraph

26
, the court cited the following general definition of the doctrine parliamentary
privilege, which is found in
Parliamentary Privilege in Canada (1982),

J.P.Joseph Maingot, Q.C. at p. 12:

Parliamentary privilege is the
necessary immunity that the law provides for members of Parliament, and for
members of the legislatures of each of the ten provinces and two territories,
in order for these legislators to do their legislative work.  It is
also the necessary immunity that the law provides for anyone while taking
part in a proceeding in Parliament or in a legislature. Finally, it is the
authority and power of each House of Parliament and of each legislature to
enforce that immunity.

[
142
]

Mr. Desrosiers
testified in his capacity as the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly for
Ontario.  As such, he is the “principal authority on the law, practices and
privileges of Parliament.”  (See Tab A of his Affidavit, which is Exhibit 1).
Therefore, I accord substantial weight to his testimony.

[
143
]

Mr. Desrosiers said
that the privilege in issue in the case before me is that of the Speaker
ensuring that the Legislative Precinct is used in a way that is consistent with
the protection of the right of the Members to conduct their business in the
House without interference. He said that this power to regulate the use of the
Legislative Precinct is derived from “…long standing principles that the House
has devolved through the Speaker – the right to ensure that they [Members] have
access.”  He said that the Speaker’s power to exclude non-Members from parts of
the Legislative Precinct, other than the Chamber of the House, derives from
parliamentary privilege and the right of the Speaker to administer the Legislative
Building and to regulate its use and the use of the grounds.

[
144
]

In
Parliamentary
Privilege In Canada (2d),
Maingot states on page 163 that, “Each House of
Parliament has jurisdiction over its precincts.” At page 314, he lists as a
recognized parliamentary privilege, the “ejection of strangers from the House
and
its precincts
.”  (Emphasis Added)  The Supreme Court of Canada accepted
this in

New Brunswick Broadcasting
(Supra) at paragraphs 129; 134-137.

[
145
]

Based on this, I
find that the parliamentary privilege that is invoked in the case before me is
the “ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts.”

[
146
]

In the case before
me, the Defendants do not dispute that this is a recognized parliamentary
privilege, however they argue that with regard the Ontario Legislature it is
not necessary that the privilege extend to the grounds that surround the
Legislative building.  They would confine the ambit of the privilege to the
Legislative building and to the other buildings and structures used by the
Legislature, such as, Whitney Block and the tunnel that connects it to the Legislative
building.

[
147
]

The importance of
this is that the Defendants were on the grounds of the Legislative building
when the bans were issued to them, and they were banned from the grounds.  If
the Legislative Precinct of the Ontario Legislature includes the grounds
surrounding the Legislative building, this would mean that the Speaker was
acting within the bounds of his parliamentary privilege of “the ejection of
strangers from the House
and its precincts
.” His action of banning the
Defendants from the grounds would come within the ambit of the privilege and,
consequently, I would not have the jurisdiction to review it, unless I acceded
to the Defendants’s other arguments for review.  If the Legislative Precinct
does not include the grounds then I would be able to review his action of banning
the Defendants.  Therefore, it is important to determine the definition of the
Legislative Precinct of the Ontario Legislature.

What is the definition of the
Legislative Precinct for the Legislature of Ontario?

[
148
]

In
New Brunswick
Broadcasting
(Supra) Chief Justice Lamer  (as he then was) said that:

Parliamentary privilege, and
immunity with respect to the exercise of that privilege, are founded upon
necessity.  Parliamentary privilege and the breadth of individual
privileges encompassed by that term are accorded to members of the Houses of
Parliament and the legislative assemblies because they are judged necessary to
the discharge of their legislative function.  (Paragraph 31)
At paragraph 32, he pointed out that,
“… the justification of necessity is applied in a general
sense.  That is, general categories of privilege are deemed necessary
to the discharge of the Assembly's function.  Each specific instance
of the exercise of a privilege need not be shown to be necessary. “

[
149
]

Madam Justice
McLachlin (as she then was) concluded similarly that “…
Canadian
legislative bodies properly claim as inherent privileges those rights which are
necessary to their capacity to function as legislative bodies.  There
is no dispute in the case law that necessity is the test.” (Paragraph 121)
She

explained that, “It is for the
courts to determine whether necessity sufficient to support a privilege is made
out.” (Paragraph 122)

[
150
]

At
paragraph 123 she pointed out that:  “The test of necessity is not applied
as a standard for judging the content of a claimed privilege, but for the
purpose of determining the necessary sphere of exclusive or absolute
"parliamentary" or "legislative"
jurisdiction.  If a matter falls within this necessary sphere of
matters without which the dignity and efficiency of the House cannot be upheld,
courts will not inquire into questions concerning such
privilege.  All such questions will instead fall to the exclusive
jurisdiction of the legislative body.”

[
151
]

She explained this
in another way at paragraph 126
,
by saying:   “In summary, it seems clear that, from an historical
perspective, Canadian legislative bodies possess such inherent privileges as
may be necessary to their proper functioning.  These privileges are
part of the fundamental law of our land, and hence are
constitutional.  The courts may determine if the privilege claimed is
necessary to the capacity of the legislature to function, but have no power to
review the rightness or wrongness of a particular decision made pursuant to the
privilege.”

[
152
]

[
153
]

[

]

and

…under the control of
the Speaker…” (Emphasis Added)

[
155
]

on behalf of the Legislative Assembly

[

the Assembly
has control of the Legislative

and the grounds of the Legislative building

and the 1

[
159
]

The evidence shows that in signing these
Memoranda of Understanding, all of which contained this definition of the

on behalf of the Legislative
Assembly.
And further that “By Order-in-Council 957/90,
the Assembly

and the grounds of the Legislative

.”
(Emphasis Added)

,
written by the Standing Committee On The Legislative Assembly, 1
st

th

[
161
]

It is reasonable to infer from this that the

[
162
]

The Speaker is a signatory to all three
Memoranda referred to above. The Speaker’s actions through these vehicles to

[
163
]

As to necessity, one has but to look at the
evidence that was given by Mr. Desrosiers. There was no evidence that
successfully challenged or contradicted him on this issue.

[
164
]

Mr. Norris argued for the Defence that it is
not necessary for the proper functioning of Parliament that the Legislative

[

This is an interesting concession because of

[

[
167
]

In Appendix 3 of the
Report On Security
In The Legislative Precincts,
mentioned above, which is the submission to
the Committee of the Honourable Allan McLean, Speaker, he states on page 3

[

]

In a letter which letter is part of Exhibit
3, dated November 16, 1995 and written by Speaker McLean to, Mr. Arnott,

(Appendix 3 of Exhibit 3)

[

]

necessary for the proper and decorous functioning of Parliament that the

but it did not call any evidence that successfully refuted it.

[
170
]

The defence argued that Mr. Desrosiers
testified that the Memoranda of Understanding are based on s. 103 (2) of the
Legislative
Assembly Act
and that this section does not mention the grounds surrounding
the Legislative building and the Memoranda cannot on its own extend the definition
of the Legislative Precinct to include the grounds. Section 103 says:

103. --(1) Such parts of the
Legislative Building as may be designated by the Lieutenant Governor in Council
in addition to the Legislative Chamber shall be under the control of the

(2)
The Speaker shall establish guidelines for the security of the Legislative Chamber
and the other parts of the Legislative Building that are under his or her

c. L.10, s. 103
.

[
171
]

However, the Memoranda of Understanding
cites both the
Legislative Assembly Act

and
Order-in-Council No.
957/90, which states that the Legislative Precinct does include the grounds
around the Legislative building.

[
172
]

The evidence mentioned above makes it clear
that the Legislative Assembly was made aware of the definition of the
Legislative Precinct, which was mentioned in the Memoranda and in
Order-in-Council 957/90.  By adopting the
Report On Security In The Legislative
Precincts
, the Legislative Assembly confirmed and accepted that the
Memoranda of Understanding and the Order-In- Council define the Legislative
Precinct and place it under the control of the Speaker.  This definition
clearly includes the grounds around the Legislative building.

[
173
]

Mr. Norris’ argument that the Speaker’s
control over the grounds of the Legislative building does not derive from the
principle of parliamentary privilege because it depends on s.103 of the
Legislative
Assembly Act
and on Order-in-Council 957/90, is not wholly correct. First,
s.103 does not refer to the grounds.  Secondly, in an effort to provide better
security for it self and its members so that they can properly perform their
functions, the Legislative Assembly approved Order-in-Council 957/90, which
contains the contested definition of the Legislative Precinct.  Ensuring that
the Legislative Assembly can properly and with dignity perform its functions is
the core of the particular parliamentary privilege at issue in this case.

[
174
]

Moreover, this argument ignores Mr.
Desrosiers’s testimony to which I referred above where he said that:

1. The Speaker’s power to exclude
non-Members from the Legislative Precinct, other than the Chamber of the House,
derives from parliamentary privilege and the right of the Speaker to administer
the Legislative building and to regulate its use
and the use of the grounds.

(Paragraph 22, supra)

2. The power to regulate the use of
the Legislative Precinct derives from  “…long standing principles that the House
has devolved through the Speaker – the right to ensure that they have access.”
(Paragraph 23, supra)

3. The Order-in-Council was made
pursuant to
The Legislative Assembly Act
and
The Ministry of
Government Services Act
to “…reinforce the idea that the Speaker was,
indeed, responsible for these areas.” (Paragraph 27, supra)

[
175
]

In addition, as indicated above, the
evidence shows that the House, inferentially if not directly, approved of the
grounds around the Legislative building being included within the Legislative
Precinct by adopting the
Report On Security In The Legislative Precincts
.

[
176
]

The “ejection of strangers from the House
and its precincts” is one of the recognized categories of parliamentary
privilege. In the case before me the claiming of the grounds surrounding the
Legislative building as part of the Legislative Precinct pursuant to the
Order-in-Council and the Memoranda, could itself be viewed as an act of
parliamentary privilege, because it deals directly with the privilege of the
“ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts” in order to ensure the
proper and dignified functioning of the Legislative Assembly. Therefore, I find
that this argument fails.

[
177
]

Mr. Norris argued that it was not necessary
to the proper functioning of the Legislative Assembly to extend the definition
of the Legislative Precinct to the grounds surrounding the Legislative
building.  He submitted that Mr. Desrosiers’s evidence that without parliamentary
privilege over the grounds the Legislative Assembly would be vulnerable to
disruptions from demonstrations on the grounds does not make it necessary to
have the grounds included in the definition of the Legislative Precinct,
because the Metropolitan Toronto Police would be available to attend to any
problems.

[
178
]

This argument runs counter to experience.
Mr. Desrosiers testified to several incidents at Queen’s Park, which were
potentially disruptive, or actually disrupted the proper functioning of the
Legislative Assembly despite of the availability of the police to address the
problems.

[
179
]

Another example of this is in
R. v.
Casselman
[1996] O.J. No. 5343
, where the Speaker of the House of the
Ontario Legislative Assembly had to bring a motion for an interlocutory
injunction to restrain picketers “…from blocking or obstructing the entrance to
or egress from the Legislative Precinct by Members of Provincial Parliament and
essential staff of the Legislative Assembly.”  (Para. 1) The Speaker decided
that it was necessary to take this extraordinary action despite the availability
of the police to address the disruptions.

[
180
]

Mr. Norris also argued that it is
inconsistent with the underlying notions of parliamentary privilege that the
Speaker shares control over policing duties on the grounds of the Legislative
building with the Toronto police, who have a jurisdiction apart from the
Speaker to police the grounds.

[
181
]

The Legislative Assembly does not have to go
it alone in regulating behaviour in an area that it has clearly defined as its
Legislative Precinct in order to assert parliamentary privilege over that area.
There is no authority that says that it does, nor does it make sense to fetter
the Legislative Assembly in that manner. The Assembly must be left free to take
whatever action it deems necessary to ensure the proper and dignified
functioning of the Legislative Assembly, even if it involves collaboration with
the police force.

[
182
]

The Memorandum of Understanding between the
Speaker and the Metropolitan Toronto Police Service (Exhibit 1, Tab E) makes it
clear in the preamble that:

•

“…the Assembly is responsible for the security
of the Legislative Precinct comprised of the Legislative building
and the surrounding
grounds
as identified in the Order-in-Council [957/90]…”  (Emphasis Added)

•

The Metropolitan Toronto Police Service is
responsible, pursuant to the
Police Services Act, R.S.O. 1990. c.P.15
,
to
provide policing services within the Municipality of Metropolitan Toronto,
which includes the Legislative Precinct
.

•

“...the parties wish to enter into a Memorandum
of Understanding to delineate their respective responsibilities for providing
security and for policing the Legislative Precinct.”

The
preamble makes it clear that it is pursuant to its responsibility for the security
of the Legislative Precinct that the Legislative Assembly has seen fit to enter
into these arrangements.

[
183
]

The Memorandum of Understanding states the
following important things:

•

As part of its responsibility to provide
policing services within the Municipality of Metropolitan Toronto, the police
will provide “…its usual, daily policing services to those grounds surrounding
the Legislative building, as those grounds are defined in Order-in-Council No.
957/90.”

•

The Metropolitan Toronto Police Service will “…
on
a request by the Assembly
…provide such policing services as are available
in the circumstances, to address: (a) special events (i.e.) demonstrations)
which are anticipated to be held at the Legislative Precinct; and (b) emergency
situations that have arisen at the Legislative Precinct …” [Emphasis Added]

•

Once such a request is made, the police shall
have the sole discretion to determine the nature, level and extent of the
services to be provided and the appropriate deployment of police personnel and
equipment.

[
184
]

It is clear from this that the Legislative
Assembly is responsible for security within the Legislative Precinct and that
it chose to enlist the help of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Service to
assist it in this task.  The police do not have “the right” to police the
Legislative Precinct.  The
Act
is administered by the Solicitor General
(s.3 (1)), who “monitor[s] police forces to ensure that adequate and effective
police services are provided at the municipal and provincial levels.” (s.3
(2)(a)).  And it is the municipalities that “shall provide adequate and
effective police services in accordance with its needs.” (s.4 (1)) The Act
provides for various ways in which municipalities can provide this service,
many of which entail entering into agreements with existing police forces to
police their area.

[
185
]

It can be said that under this scheme the
Speaker is to a limited extent and under certain conditions, delegating his
responsibility for the security of the Legislative Precinct to the Metropolitan
Toronto Police Service.  Mr. Desrosiers testified that the police have authority
outside of the Legislative building “under the permission of the Speaker.” And
further, that this is reflected in the Memorandum of Understanding. (Page 87,
lines 28-33; page 88, lines 1-11, November 17, 2003 transcript)

[
186
]

This is the same type of delegation that
the Speaker employed with regard to the Legislative Security Service in
paragraph 1.2 of the Memorandum where it states:  “The parties further
acknowledge that the LSS is responsible for providing the usual, daily security
services inside the buildings of the Legislative Precinct.”

[
187
]

There is nothing inconsistent with the
principle of parliamentary privilege in doing this.  The Speaker has simply
taken these actions in order to comply with his duty to provide adequate
security for the proper and dignified functioning of the Legislative Assembly;
and as such, they are within the ambit of parliamentary privilege.

[
188
]

I find support for this conclusion in
Parliamentary
Privilege in Canada, second edition
, J.P. Joseph Maingot, Q.C., at page171.
Mr. Maingot states:

The
security of the buildings occupied by Members comes under the Protective
Service of the House of Commons because the House alone may regulate its own
affairs and its own proceedings within its own walls.  Standing Order 157 (2)
provides that the Sergeant-at-Arms “preserves order in the galleries,
corridors, lobbies and other parts.” (There is no mention here of the area
outside the buildings.)
Should events occur inside the buildings that would
require further help,
it is arranged
that the security staff will ask
for and receive assistance form the RCMP and/or the city police. Because the
administration of justice is a provincial responsibility, any breaches of the
Criminal
Code
within the precincts will be prosecuted by the Crown Attorney for the
Judicial District of Ottawa-Carleton.
(Emphasis Added)

[
189
]

It certainly cannot be argued that by making
this arrangement the Speaker of the House of Commons is acting in a manner that
is inconsistent with his parliamentary privilege to exercise control over the
part of the Legislative Precinct that is situated “inside the buildings”, and
that he or she no longer enjoys parliamentary privilege inside the buildings of
the House of Commons.  Similarly, the Speaker of the Ontario Legislature
“arranged” in the Memoranda of Understanding discussed above, that in certain
circumstances and under certain conditions the Metropolitan Toronto Police
Services will aid the Speaker in exercising control over the Legislative
Precinct.

[
190
]

The defence also argued that: (1) I can and
should examine the parliamentary privilege that the Speaker relies on in
issuing the
Trespass To Property Act
bans to determine if its breadth is
necessary to the proper functioning of Parliament, and (2) that such an inquiry
should be temporally relevant to the present taking into account that the law
evolves and, therefore, could have departed from what it was in the past.

[
191
]

Considering my findings above, the first
argument has been disposed of against the Defendants.

[
192
]

Regarding the second argument, I would refer
to the Court of Appeal for Ontario’s decision in
Telezone
(supra), at
paragraph 45, where it dealt with these issues.
The court framed the issues thusly, “
The
respondent contends that the court must review the parliamentary privilege as
so defined and determine whether it is necessary to the proper functioning of
Parliament. Moreover, the respondent submits that the temporal context for this
inquiry is today, not the time at which the privilege was created nor the time
it may have arisen in Canada.”

[
193
]

The issue in
Telezone
was whether or not it was
necessary for parliamentary privilege to exempt Members of Parliament from
testifying for the entire session of Parliament and during the 40 days that
follow the session, and the 40 days before the next session starts. The defence
pointed out that the effect of this rule is that in the past 20 years there
have been only four brief time periods, which totaled 138 days, during which
Members of Parliament could have been summonsed to court to testify.

[
194
]

As in the case before me, the defence argued that “a
privilege with such a sweeping scope is not necessary to the proper functioning
of Parliament.” (Paragraph 47)

[
195
]

Mr. Justice Macpherson, writing for the majority, held at
paragraph 48 that these arguments misconceived “both the nature of the
necessity inquiry in which a court might engage and the temporal context of
that inquiry.”  He cited
New Brunswick Broadcasting
(supra), at page 383
where McLachlin J. (as she then was) said:

The test
of necessity is not applied as a standard for judging the
content
of a
claimed privilege, but for the purpose of determining the necessary sphere of
exclusive or absolute "parliamentary" or "legislative"
jurisdiction. If a matter falls within this necessary
sphere of matters

without which the dignity and efficiency of the House cannot be upheld, courts
will not inquire into questions concerning such privilege. All such questions
will instead fall to the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislative body. (Emphasis
Added)

[
196
]

Macpherson J.A., held, at paragraph 51, that
it was a question for Parliament, not the courts.  He said that, “ Once a court
has determined that a parliamentary privilege exists and has ascertained its
definition or scope, its role ends.  He cited
New Brunswick Broadcasting

(supra), at page 387-88 to support this conclusion:

But,
it is argued, it is not necessary that the right be absolute. The courts
should be given the power to monitor the exercise of this power to ensure
that only those strangers who are truly disruptive are excluded. In my view,
a system of court review, quite apart from the constitutional question of
what right the courts have to interfere in the internal process of another
branch of government, would bring its own problems. The ruling of the
Assembly would not be final. The Assembly would find itself caught up in
legal proceedings and appeals about what is disruptive and not disruptive.
This in itself might impair the proper functioning of the chamber. This lends
support to the venerable and accepted proposition that it is necessary to the
proper functioning of a legislative assembly modeled on the Parliamentary
system of the United Kingdom that the Assembly possess the absolute right to
exclude strangers from its proceedings, when it deems them to be disruptive
of its efficacious operation.

[
197
]

Further, with regard to the temporal context
issue Macpherson, J.A. said:

With
respect to the temporal context of the necessity inquiry, for the federal Parliament
it is clearly July 1, 1867 by virtue of
s. 18
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
and
s. 4 of the Parliament of Canada Act. These constitutional and statutory
provisions envisage
the possibility
of a different time period being
relevant, but only if Parliament enacts a law dealing with a privilege sometime
after 1867. That has not happened with respect to the privilege relating to
testimonial immunity. (Paragraph 50)  (Emphasis in original)

[
198
]

In the case before me, there have not been
any changes made to the parliamentary privilege of, “ejection of strangers from
the House and its precincts
”.
The evolution of the human rights law, as
seen for example in
The Charter of Rights And Freedoms
, has not caused
Parliament to modify this privilege to allow review of it under the
Charter

or any other human rights legislation.  Other that
Vaid
, (supra) there
is no case that has undertaken such a task.  And as pointed out by Ms. Beagan
Flood, counsel for the Speaker,
Vaid
goes against all of the other
jurisprudence in this area, much of which was decided after the
Charter
and
other recent human rights legislation came into force.

[
199
]

Consequently, I conclude that to date, the
privilege of “ejection of strangers from the House and its precincts
”
is
in force as it always has been and I do not agree that the
Charter
or
any other human rights legislation can modify it.

[
200
]

Mr. Norris’s final argument on the issue of
parliamentary privilege is that the Speaker cannot shelter under parliamentary
privilege because he resorted to the
Trespass To Property Act
to issue
the bans,

and to the police and the courts to enforce them. Thus, the
Speaker does not exercise his own powers to enforce the bans.

[
201
]

It is imaginative and skilful of Mr. Norris
to characterize this issuance of the bans as resorting to the
Trespass To
Property Act
.  However, if one looks at the bans that were issued (Exhibit
1, Tabs L to P), they simply say
:  “Effective, today you are prohibited to
enter on the premises of the Legislative Precinct, Queen’s Park which includes
the Main Legislative building and the Whitney Block.  Any contravention of this
order will result in charges being laid against you under the Trespass To
Property Act.”
Given the evidence cited above one should add to the last
sentence “at the discretion of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Service.”

[
202
]

It could be inferred that by issuing the
bans the Speaker availed himself of the
Trespass To Property Act
,
because the letter says that if the ban is not obeyed, charges will be laid
under the
Trespass To Property Act.
However, that is not the only
inference that can be drawn. In the circumstances of the case before me,
considering the evidence adduced, I find that the implication of this letter is
that the Speaker resorted to his parliamentary privilege to ban the Defendants.
I do not interpret the letter as meaning that the Speaker resorted to the

Trespass To Property Act.
There is nowhere in the letter that it says that
the bans are issued pursuant to the
Trespass To Property Act,
because
the Speaker does not need the
Act
in order to ban the Defendants.

[
203
]

Furthermore, the evidence shows clearly that
the Speaker does not have any role in deciding to charge and/or prosecute
persons that are arrested for trespassing in the Legislative Precinct.  This is
the domain of the police and of the Crown.  Therefore, it is not accurate to
say that the Speaker invokes the processes of the court in order to enforce the
bans. The Speaker would not be a party to this case had not the Defendants
challenged his authority to issue the bans and contested the description of the
Legislative Precinct.  In fact, the Speaker was allowed to participate in these
proceedings solely for the purpose of addressing these issues.  He has no
interest in the prosecution of the charges.  That is the job of the Crown, who
is ably represented in the proceedings by Mr. Galligan and Mr. Guttman.

[
204
]

I agree with Ms. Beagan Flood’s argument
stated at paragraph 63 of her Factum, that once I decide that the Speaker was
acting within the ambit of a recognized parliamentary privilege when he issued
the bans, his actions are beyond
Charter
scrutiny.  And invoking the
court’s processes cannot give me jurisdiction to review an act that is not
subject to the
Charter.
As she submitted in paragraph 66 of her Factum
citing,
Ontario (Speaker of the Legislative Assembly)

(Supra) @31,

(which actually is @ paragraph 32),

“The
Charter

recognizes

Parliamentary Privilege, it does not
override
it.” (Emphasis Added)

[
205
]

In addition, Mr. Norris concedes that in
Ontario
(Speaker of the Legislative Assembly) v. Casselman,
[1996] O.J. No. 5343
(Ont.
Ct. (Gen. Div.))(QL)
the Speaker asked the court to issue an injunction
against OPSEU picketers at Queen’s Park and this did not oust the Speaker’s
parliamentary privilege. Mr. Norris tried to distinguish the case by saying
that the request of the court was limited to restraining them from blocking
access and egress to two doors of the Legislative building, not to prevent them
from picketing all together. He seems to be arguing that invoking the courts
assistance does not oust the Speaker’s parliamentary privilege if it is a
“limited invoking”.

[
206
]

I am not persuaded by this argument. If
invoking the courts processes is what ousts the Speaker’s parliamentary
privilege, then it should not matter whether the court is being asked to
address a specific or a general situation.  I would also point out that
although the defence has very adeptly tried to portray the bans in question in
the case at bar as bans “against demonstrating”, they were not. They were bans
against being on the grounds of the Legislative building.  A
consequence

of that is that the Defendants could not go there to demonstrate (or for any
other purpose), but that does not mean that the bans were bans “against demonstrating”.

[
207
]

There is another way of looking at Mr.
Norris’s argument. Under the
Trespass to Property Act
it is the
“occupier” of premises or lands that has the authority to issue bans. Although
the Act does not say this expressly, that is the clear implication of sections
1(a), (b); 2 (1); 3 (1); 8, and 9.

[
208
]

Section 1 of the Act defines “occupier” as
follows:

1. --(1) In this Act,

"occupier" includes,

(a) a person who is
in
physical possession of premises
, or

(b)

a person who has
responsibility
for and control over the condition of premises or the activities there
carried on, or control over persons allowed to enter the premises,

even if there is more than one
occupier of the same premises;  (Emphasis Added)

[
209
]

Given the definition of “occupier”, if as
Mr. Norris argues, the Speaker resorted to the
Act
to issue the bans it
would mean that he had to be the “occupier” of the grounds around the
Legislative building in order to do so.  And according to the
Act
, that
would mean that he had “physical possession” of, or that he had the “
responsibility for and control over the
condition of premises or the activities there carried on, or control over
persons allowed to enter the premises”, which is exactly what the Speaker is
arguing in this case.  Therefore, his alleged resorting to the
Act
to
issue the bans would itself be an act of his parliamentary privilege and could
not be reviewed by me.

[
210
]

Regarding the Defendant, Mr. Behrens’s,
argument that the Speaker has absolute, unaccountable power and immunity under
the guise of parliamentary privilege, I would point out that it is clear that
when the Speaker acts under parliamentary privilege, his or her actions are
reviewable by the Legislative Assembly.  The courts also have a reviewing power
in so far as they can determine if a Speaker goes outside of the parliamentary
privilege that he or she invokes.  Therefore, I do not think that Speakers can
do what ever they want under the guise of parliamentary privilege, nor do I
think that they have an unreviewable discretion to make any activity with which
they disagree the subject of a prosecution in court, as Mr. Behrens fears.

[
211
]

Next, he submitted that in the case at bar
the Speaker used parliamentary privilege for an unconstitutional end, which is
to prevent the Defendants from demonstrating on the grounds of the Legislative
building.  As I stated above in paragraph 206, I do not agree with this
argument.

[
212
]

Mr. Behrens also submitted that the doctrine
of parliamentary privilege prevents the Defendants from reviewing this exercise
of the Speaker’s parliamentary privilege.  However, the law set down by the
Supreme Court of Canada is that the courts do not have the jurisdiction to
review exercises of parliamentary privilege.  I am bound by that ruling.

[
213
]

Mr. Behrens was also concerned that no one
would be able to question and determine whether or not the Speaker was truly
honourable, just, and acted in keeping with the
Charter of Rights And
Freedoms
and the
Constitution.
As explained above, the way that our
legal system works is that, even if the Speaker is acting within the ambit of
parliamentary privilege, the Legislative Assembly can review his or her
actions.

[
214
]

I denote a fear on the part of some of the
Defendants that Speakers of Legislative Assemblies in Canada will abuse their
privileges to the detriment of the public unless their actions are reviewable
by the courts under the
Charter
and other human rights legislation.
This is a legitimate concern, in theory at least, but no examples of this type
of abuse were presented to me as evidence.  It is instructive to recall what
Madam Justice McLachlin said in this regard in
New Brunswick Broadcasting
(Supra):

… the
historical record suggests that the danger of abuse of the Speaker's power to
control proceedings in the House, even to the point of excluding strangers, is
not grave.  The right to exclude strangers has been recognized in the
United Kingdom for centuries and in this country for well over one hundred
years without adverse effect.  And the legislative assembly always
faces the ultimate sanction, that of the voters. (Paragraph
140)

[
215
]

The courts are
aware of the importance of protecting individual rights against abuses by state
agencies.  In
The Legislative Prayer Case
(Supra at paragraph 246) the
court referred to Madam Justice McLachlin’s judgment in
Harvey v. New Brunswick
(Attorney General),
1996 CanLII 163 (SCC)
,
[1996] 2 S.C.R. 876
,
178 N.B.R. (2d) 161
,
137 D.L.R. (4
th
)
142
,
201 N.R. 1
,
454, A.P.R. 161
,
37 C.R.R. (2d) 189
where she said at page
918 S.C.R.:

This is
not to say that the courts have no role to play in the debate which arises
where individual rights are alleged to conflict with parliamentary privilege.
Under the British system of parliamentary supremacy, the courts arguably play
no role in monitoring the exercise of parliamentary privilege. In Canada, this
has been altered by the
Charter
's enunciation of values which may in particular
cases conflict with the exercise of such privilege. To prevent abuses cloaked
in the guise of privilege from trumping legitimate Charter interests, the
courts must inquire into the legitimacy of a claim of parliamentary privilege.
As this Court made clear in New Brunswick Broadcasting, the courts may properly
question whether a claimed privilege exists.

This screening role means
that where it is alleged that a person has been expelled or disqualified on
invalid grounds, the courts must determine whether the act falls within the
scope of parliamentary privilege. If the court concludes that it does, no
further review lies.

[
216
]

evidence that Toronto Action For Social Change interfered with the functioning

The main
attack on Thompson's [the plaintiff] action is the argument that the court has

[
218
]

allowed to proceed to trial and have the trial judge determine if parliamentary

The test
is functional; would it interfere with the essential parliamentary functions of

There may
be cases where this functional test can be applied in a factual vacuum on the

]

claim,
without examining at trial the evidence on which the claim of privilege

[
220
]

is clearly distinguishable from the case before me.  The court was

[
221
]

222

224
]

]

227
]

to stage a demonstration are asked to comply with the guidelines. And even if

228

[

Finally, Ms. Hiscocks asked me to strike a
balance between the
Charter of Rights And Freedoms
and the doctrine of
parliamentary privilege. She underlined that the case at bar is about the

Charter
rights are
involved.  I think that Ms. Hiscocks has put her finger on a very important

230

The Legislative Prayer Case
(Supra) referred to the issue of the dynamic between
Charter

Earlier in that decision [
Harvey (
Supra)],
McLachlin J. dealt specifically with the argument that parliamentary privilege

Charter
violation. McLachlin J.

Because parliamentary privilege enjoys constitutional
status it is not “subject to “ the
Charter
,
as                    are
ordinary laws. Both parliamentary privilege and the
Charter
constitute
essential parts of the                        Constitution of Canada.  Neither
prevails over the other.  While parliamentary privilege
and                             immunity from improper judicial interference in
parliamentary processes must be maintained, so                      must the
fundamental democratic guarantees of the
Charter.
Where apparent
conflicts between                       different constitutional principles
arise, the proper approach is not to resolve the conflict
by                              subordinating one principle to the other, but
rather to attempt to reconcile them.

The Court of Appeal noted that,
“…the reconciliation process referenced by McLachlin J. involves reading the

Charter
as being consistent with parliamentary privilege, not the other way
around as submitted by the appellant. The Charter recognizes Parliamentary
privilege, it does not override it.”

The
Legislative Precinct In Other Jurisdictions

[
231
]

For the purpose of comparison, I researched
the other Provinces and the three Territories to see how their legislatures
define their Legislative Precincts.  The results are not binding or dispositive
of the issues before me, but I think that it is useful to see what other
jurisdictions have done in this respect.

[
232
]

Some of the material that I found is hearsay
from the Clerk of the Legislature, the legislative librarian, or in one case
(Newfoundland), the Speaker himself.  I did not consider this information and I
will not refer to it.  I will refer only to those jurisdictions that have enacted
legislation in which the Legislative Precinct is defined.

[
233
]

I was able to find useful material with
regard to two of the Provinces and one of the Territories (British Columbia,
Nova Scotia and Nunavut).  In addition, Ms. Beagan Flood provided the court
with Australian legislation from the state Parliaments of New South Wales,
Queensland, the Northern Territory, Tasmania, Western Australia, and South
Australia.  They all show that their the Legislative Precincts include the

opportunity to see these materials and to make submissions on them.

[
234
]

In British Columbia, pursuant to the
Legislative
Assembly Management Committee Act, chapter 258,
the Legislative Precinct
includes the Parliament Buildings and the legislative grounds and Confederation

[
235
]

In Nova Scotia, under Rule 7 of the Rules
and Forms of Procedure of the House of Assembly, “The Speaker shall have

pointed out to me in her submissions that the
House of Assembly Act, R.S.N.S.
1989 (1992 Supp.), c. 1, s.32 (3)
provides that: “All rules of the House
not inconsistent with this Act have the force and effect of law until altered,
amended or repealed.”

[
236
]

In Nunavut, the
Legislative Assembly and
Executive Council Act,
s. 8 (1) describes the Legislative Precinct as
follows:  “In Iqaluit, the precinct of the Legislative Assembly is under the

and any other office, warehouse or storage space ordinarily and commonly used

temporarily used by the members and the officers and employees of the Office of
the Legislative Assembly for the business of the Legislative Assembly.

[
237
]

When the Legislative Assembly sits outside
of Iqaluit, the Legislative Precinct “…is under the jurisdiction of the

[
238
]

In
Parliamentary Privilege in Canada (2d)

(Supra), Maingot remarks at page 175 that the precincts in England, “are
considered to be the area within the walls of the Palace of Westminster, and,
by virtue of their corporate occupation by the Commons, the outbuildings used
by Members."  It was explained by Mr. Desrosiers that there are no grounds
at the Palace of Westminster because it faces the Thames.

[
239
]

Maingot points out on pages 175,176 that: “
In New Zealand, “precincts” of Parliament probably include the grounds, because
while Parliament is in session, the control and administration of the grounds

dissolution, the control reverts to the government.” Indeed, the
Parliamentary
Service Act 2000,
s. 3 confirms this.

[
240
]

In Australia, the
Legislative Assembly
Precincts Act 2001 (A.C.T.),
ss. 5, 7, and 9 provide that the Legislative
Precinct includes the grounds around the Legislature.  The definition is long
and it is not necessary to repeat it here.  It is interesting to note that this
legislation is contrary to what Maingot states at page 176 about the boundaries
of the Legislative Precinct in Australia. He cites the Speaker of the House of
Representatives where he said that the Speaker’s authority ends at the outer
walls of the building.  The reference is
Australia Parliamentary Debates
(1950-51)
, p. 331.  Maingot cites the
Minutes & Proceedings of
Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization of the House of Commons
,
May 24, 1973 for a more updated definition which states that “any place
de
facto
occupied by Members for their parliamentary duties is part of the precincts…”.

[
241
]

Ms. Beagan Flood submits that I can take
judicial notice of the above-mentioned legislation.  She cites the
Evidence
Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.E.23
, ss. 25-
28
; R
. v. St. Lawrence Cement Inc.

(2002),
2002 CanLII 45010 (ON CA)
,
60 O.R. (3d) 712
@ 717-19,
and S.C. Hill, D. Tanovich, L. Strezos
and S.C. Hutchinson,
McWilliams’ Canadian Criminal Evidence, 4
th

ed. (Aurora, Ontario: Canada Law Book, 2004) @ 23-61 to 23-62
, in support
of this argument.  I reviewed these authorities and I agree with her that I can
take judicial notice of the above-mentioned legislation, including the foreign
