evidence in order to take judicial notice of this legislation.

[
242
]

The above cited legislation shows that the
Ontario Legislature, in defining the Legislative Precinct as including the
grounds surrounding the Legislative building, is in step with other Canadian
and Commonwealth jurisdictions.

Disposition

I considered all of the
evidence, the relevant law, and all of the submissions made by the parties.
Based on this I find that:

(1)

It is necessary for the
dignified and
proper
functioning of the Legislature of Ontario that the Speaker have control over
the grounds surrounding the Legislative building, and for the Legislative Precinct
to be defined so as to cover this area.

(2)

This control comes within, and forms part of, the Speaker’s
parliamentary            privilege of the “ejection of strangers from the House
and its precincts”, because it is necessary in order to ensure that nothing
that occurs within the Legislative Precinct that impedes the proper functioning
of the Legislative Assembly.

(14)

The Legislative
Precinct for the Legislature of Ontario is as it is defined in Order-in-Council
957/90 as being “…the entire Legislative building, the grounds bounded on the
east by Queen’s Park Crescent East, on the north by Wellesley Street West and
on the west by Queen’s Park Crescent West, and the first and second floors of
the Whitney Block;”

•

And in addition,
covers the added areas that the Speaker confirmed in a Memorandum of
Understanding between the Ministry of Government Of [sic] Services and The Office
of the Assembly, which was revised on October 15, 1992.  At paragraph 2.1 of
said Memorandum, “the tunnel connecting the Legislative building to the Whitney
Block; and the third floor and part of the basement of the Whitney Block “ were
added.  (See Exhibit I, Tab D, Affidavit of Mr. Desrosiers)

(3)

This was the area in which the Defendants
were demonstrating when the
Trespass to Property Act
bans were issued to
them, and the area to which the bans refer.

(4)

The exterior wall of the Legislative
building is a part of the building, and therefore, even taking the definition
of the precinct urged on me by the defence, it is within the precinct,
and the Defendants went into it when they
poured the stage blood on the building.

(5)

The reasons that
the bans were issued to the Defendants were:

•

Inspector Beale
asked the group with which the Defendants were demonstrating to leave several
times and they did not;

•

It was believed by
the Legislative Security Services that they defaced the Legislative building
with the blood-like substance;

•

The area of the
Legislature where the demonstration was taking place was not accessible from
that side.

Was
The Speaker Acting Within The Bounds Of Parliamentary Privilege When He Issued
The Trespass To Property Bans To The Defendants?

[
243
]

In
New Brunswick Broadcasting
(Supra)
the court said: “In summary, it seems clear that, from an historical
perspective, Canadian legislative bodies possess such inherent privileges as
may be necessary to their proper functioning.  These privileges are
part of the fundamental law of our land, and hence are
constitutional.   The courts may determine if the privilege claimed
is necessary to the capacity of the legislature to function, but have no power
to review the rightness or wrongness of a particular decision made pursuant to
the privilege. (Para. 126)
Each
specific instance of the exercise of a privilege need not be shown to be
necessary. (Para. 32)

[
244
]

In Ontario (Speaker of the Legislative
Assembly) v. Ontario (Human Rights Commission) (2001),
2001 CanLII 8549 (ON CA)
, 54 O.R. (3d) 595 (C.A.)
the court held at paragraph 25 that:

… while it is true to
say in the abstract that parliamentary privilege covers those matters which are
necessary to the functioning of the House, "necessity" in this
context applies to categories of matters, and each particular exercise of
privilege within a category is not scrutinized against a standard of necessity.
As noted by McLachlin J., once a court has decided that a category of matters
is necessary to the independent functioning of the House, it does not then go
on to decide whether each individual exercise of privilege is necessary, but,
rather, only has to ask whether the particular exercise in question falls
within the recognized category of privilege. If it does, it is not subject to
outside review.

[
245
]

Parliamentary privilege enjoys
constitutional status.
New Brunswick Broadcasting
(Supra) at paragraph
117.  At paragraph 144, the court held that one part of the Constitution cannot
abrogate another part of the Constitution.

[
246
]

Above, I found that the Legislative Precinct
for the Legislature of Ontario includes the grounds around the Legislative
building.  The evidence shows that the Defendants were in the Legislative Precinct
when the bans were issued.

[
247
]

Therefore, based on the reasons given
above I find that the Speaker was acting within the bounds of a recognized
category of parliamentary privilege, which was: the “ejection of strangers from
the House and its precincts”, when he issued the bans.

[
248
]

Mr. Norris argued that pursuant to
Vaid

(Supra) I can step in and determine if this particular exercise of
parliamentary privilege stands up to scrutiny.

[
249
]

In that case, pursuant to the exercise of
his staff managerial function, the Speaker declared Mr. Vaid surplus.  He had
worked as a chauffer for the Speaker of the House of Commons.  Mr. Vaid made a
complaint under the
Canadian Human Rights Act
.  The Speaker raised
parliamentary privilege, but the court held that it did not apply.  The court
said, “…parliamentary privilege does not extend to an exercise of managerial
powers involving human rights violations as presently alleged which…if proven
diminish the dignity and integrity of the House without improving its
functioning.”  (Paragraph 42)

[
250
]

In
Vaid

the court read down the
parliamentary privilege in issue so that it would not apply to a human rights
violation that occurred in the exercise of what was a recognized area of
parliamentary privilege.
Vaid
says that there is no parliamentary privilege
to discriminate against people.

[
251
]

The issue in
Vaid
was “whether the
Human Rights Commission is permitted to investigate an allegation of
discrimination by a discharged employee of the House of Commons against the
former Speaker of the House, or whether parliamentary privilege blocks such an
inquiry.” (Paragraph 1) I read carefully Létourneau J.A.’s decision, but with
great respect, I find the
ratio
unclear.

[
252
]

The parliamentary privilege in issue was the
privilege relating to control and management of the House of Commons staff.  In
expressing his concerns that this privilege not be too broad, Létourneau J.A.
observed that: “The need for a conservative rather than broad interpretation of
the parliamentary privilege as it relates to control and management of the
staff, i.e., control of the internal affairs or what the appellants termed the
"inner workings of the House of Commons" … has also been stressed in
England.” (Paragraph 28)

[
253
]

At paragraph 29, he referred to, “an article
entitled "Labour Law, Parliamentary Staff and Parliamentary
Privilege" (1983), 12 Industrial Law Journal 28, at page 37, [where] the author,
G. F. Lock, concluded that "[s]taff employment rights
are a field very
remote from the original purpose of this aspect of privilege -- the
preservation of M.P.'s freedom of speech, -- and the exclusion of staff matters
from the category 'internal affairs of the House' would not impair the rights
which the House actually needs to function"
. (Emphasis Added)

[
254
]

Létourneau J.A. also considered a Report by
the House of Lords and the House of Commons on Parliamentary Privilege, in
which “the authors, dealing with the right of each House to administer its
internal affairs within its precincts, criticized the vagueness of terms like
"control of internal affairs" (Paragraph 30)

[
255
]

At paragraph 31, he noted that the Report
concluded, “that management functions relating to the provision of services in
either House are only exceptionally subject to privilege. In particular, the
activities of the House of Commons Commission, a statutory body appointed under
the House of Commons Administration Act 1978,
are not generally subject to
privilege, nor are the management and administration of the House departments.

(Emphasis Added)

[
256
]

In these excerpts Létourneau J.A. appears to
be questioning the existence of the privilege itself.  However, I find that his
reasons can also be interpreted as simply being concerned with the privilege
being defined in too broad a manner and with how it is exercised.  This is the
direction in which his summation appears to point where he says:

To sum up,
the necessity test
in defining the scope
of the parliamentary privilege
of the House of Commons to manage and control its staff means that the
existence
and the exercise of the rights claimed to be part of the privilege

must be necessary to ensure the proper functioning of the House and
maintain its dignity and integrity. It means that such powers cannot escape the
scrutiny of the courts or other review mechanisms
when exercised
unnecessarily
because they then fall outside the scope of the privilege
delimited by the necessity. Applying this conclusion to the facts of the present
case, it means that the parliamentary privilege claimed with respect to staff
management does not preclude a review of the necessity to possess
and
exercise
the privilege where there is an allegation of racial or ethnic discrimination
contrary to the
Charter
or the CHRA. In my view, the scope of the privilege
does not extend to
an exercise
of managerial powers involving human
rights violations as presently alleged which in fact, if proven, diminish the
dignity and integrity of the House without improving its functioning.
(Paragraph 42)
(Emphasis Added)

[
257
]

But in his conclusion at paragraph 64, he
seems to revert to questioning whether the privilege exists at all when he
says:

The
privilege here asserted by the appellants to control and manage the staff of
the House of Commons would be a considerable extension of the members' right to
freedom of expression and of Parliament's original right to initially control
its proceedings. The CHRA is a fundamental law of Canada that guarantees the
right to work free from discrimination. I need not discourse on the importance
that citizens attach to their right to work and fulfill their aspirations in
life. In assessing the interests at stake, considerable weight ought to be
given to the special nature of human rights legislation which emanates from
Parliament itself.

But then at paragraph 65, he speaks
of “the scope of the parliamentary privilege “.

[
258
]

Rothstein J.A., in his reasons is clearly
concerned only with the scope of the privilege.  At paragraph 78 he states:

I accept
that the judicial branch of government must exercise considerable restraint
when faced with questions involving encroachment on the autonomy of the
legislative branch. However, I do not agree with the argument of the appellant
and Ontario Speaker that the Court must accept that the relevant
scope of
privilege
in respect of the appointment and control of staff includes any
conceivable matter that may fall under that rubric. The Court is entitled to
inquire into
the scope
of appointment and control of staff, that is,
what the term covers. Matters which fall outside the rules necessary for the
dignified and efficient functioning of Parliament will not be privileged.
(Emphasis Added)

[
259
]

Mr. Norris concedes that
Vaid
is only
about the necessity test. The court was deciding whether it was necessary to
violate Mr. Vaid’s rights in the exercise of a parliamentary privilege function
like staffing.  Mr. Norris submits that placing unreasonable limitations on the

Charter
rights of the Defendants cannot enhance the dignity and
integrity of the Ontario Legislature. He argues that the court in
Vaid

did not pass judgement over an act of the Speaker that was done within the
scope of an area of recognized parliamentary privilege; it simply went in to
define its scope.

[
260
]

As is typical for Mr. Norris, this is an
adroit argument, but I cannot agree. I find it hard to see a difference.  The
scope of that particular privilege extends to matters that deal with staffing.
It is apparent that declaring that Mr.Vaid was surplus was an act that dealt
with staffing, and hence, within that scope. Therefore, reviewing that act
under the guise of making it pass muster under human rights legislation, is
clearly passing judgement on an act of the Speaker that was done within the
scope of a particular parliamentary privilege.

[
261
]

With great respect for the Federal Court of
Appeal, what they did is exactly what the Supreme Court of Canada said no court
should do.  This is evident from the following excerpts from
New Brunswick
Broadcasting (
Supra).

•

The test of necessity
is not applied as a standard for judging the content of a claimed privilege,
but for the purpose of determining the necessary sphere of exclusive or
absolute "parliamentary" or "legislative"
jurisdiction.  If
a matter
falls within this necessary
sphere
of matters
without which the dignity and efficiency of the House cannot be
upheld, courts will not inquire into questions concerning such
privilege.  All such questions will instead fall to the exclusive
jurisdiction of the legislative body.
(Paragraph 123)

(Emphasis Added)

•

As noted above,
Stockdale v. Hansard is the leading case.  The court there rejected
the argument that the courts will take cognizance of questions involving
privilege only where the question was "incidentally" rather than
"directly" before them.  It was held that the courts were
bound to decide an issue of privilege, however it arose, but that this decision
must be subject
to the recognition of an exclusive parliamentary
jurisdiction.
The parameters of this jurisdiction are set by
what is necessary to the legislative body's capacity to function.  So
defined, the principle of necessity will encompass not only certain claimed
privileges, but also the power to determine, adjudicate upon and apply those
privileges.  Were the courts to examine
the content of particular
exercises of valid privilege, and hold some of these exercises invalid,

they would trump the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislative body, after
having admitted that the privilege in issue falls within the exclusive
jurisdiction of the legislative body.  The only area for court review
is at the initial jurisdictional level:  is
the privilege

claimed one of those privileges necessary to the capacity of the legislature to
function?

A particular
exercise of a necessary privilege
cannot
then be reviewed, unless the deference and the conclusion reached at the
initial stage be rendered nugatory.  (Paragraph 125) (Emphasis Added)

•

The courts may
determine if
the privilege claimed is necessary
to the capacity of the
legislature to function, but have no power to review the rightness or wrongness

of a particular decision made pursuant to the privilege
. (Paragraph 126)
(Emphasis Added)

•

But, it is argued, it
is not necessary that the right be absolute.  The courts should be
given the power to monitor the exercise of this power to ensure that only those
strangers who are truly disruptive are excluded.  In my view, a
system of court review, quite apart from the constitutional question of what
right the courts have to interfere in the internal process of another branch of
government, would bring its own problems.  The ruling of the Assembly
would not be final.  The Assembly would find itself caught up in
legal proceedings and appeals about what is disruptive and not disruptive.  This
in itself might impair the proper functioning of the chamber.  This
lends support to the venerable and accepted proposition that it is necessary to
the proper functioning of a legislative assembly modeled on the Parliamentary
system of the United Kingdom that the Assembly possess the absolute right to exclude
strangers from its proceedings, when it deems them to be disruptive of its
efficacious operation. (Paragraph 138) (Emphasis Added)

[
262
]

In addition to the above,
Vaid
is
distinguishable from the case before me in the sense that there is no doubt
that the parliamentary privilege to eject strangers from the House and its
precincts exists. Also, the action of the Speaker in banning the Defendants
from grounds of Legislature was an unambiguous exercise of that power.  The
Defendants do not question whether banning persons from the Legislative
Precinct falls within that privilege, rather they question whether or not the
privilege was exercised within the Legislative Precinct.   And in addition,
they turn to
Vaid
and argue that even if it was,
the banning
was
not covered by the privilege because it does not meet the necessity test.

[
263
]

With great respect to the Federal Court of
Appeal, and to the Defendants, I agree with counsel for the Speaker, Ms. Beagan
Flood, that
Vaid

is wrongly decided, because the control and management
of the House of Commons staff is a parliamentary privilege and exercises of the
privilege are not reviewable by the court.  It goes against the established
case law. Just to name a few cases, see:
New Brunswick Broadcasting

(Supra),
Ontario (Speaker of the Legislative Assembly) v. Ontario (Human
Rights Commission)

(2001),
2001 CanLII 8549 (ON CA)
,
54 O.R. (3d) 595 (C.A.)
, also known as
The
Legislative Prayer Case
, and
Telezone Inc. v.
Canada (Attorney General)

2004 CanLII 36102 (ON CA)
,
[2004] O.J. No. 5
,
235 D.L.R. (4th) 719
(2004), 180
O.A.C. 360.
I think that
the decision of whether or not it was appropriate to declare Mr. Vaid surplus,
had to be left up to the Legislature.

[
264
]

In
Ontario
(Speaker of the Legislative Assembly) v. Ontario (Human Rights Commission)

(2001),
2001 CanLII 8549 (ON CA)
,
54 O.R. (3d) 595 (C.A.)
, also known as
The
Legislative Prayer Case
(mentioned in
Vaid
, at paragraph
19
, but not
analysed) the Ontario Human Rights Commission argued that it had the
jurisdiction under the
Ontario Human Rights Code,
R.S.O. 1990, c. H.1
,
to
review Standing Order Of the House 8 (c), which provided that "[t]he
Speaker shall take the chair at the time appointed on every day fixed for the
meeting of the House and shall read the Prayers".  The Commission
submitted that it had the jurisdiction to review the Speaker’s action pursuant
to this Standing Order because his actions were alleged to violate the
Ontario
Human Rights Code.

[
265
]

At paragraph 2, the Court set out the
complaint as follows:

Mr.
Freitag filed a complaint with the Commission alleging that the recital of the
Lord's Prayer, as part of the daily opening exercise of the Ontario Legislative
Assembly … constituted a breach of his right to equal treatment with respect to
services, without discrimination because of creed, as protected by s. 1 of the
[Human Rights] Code. Mr. Freitag -- who is not a member of the Legislative
Assembly, nor subject to its internal rules -- describes himself as a
"person of non-Christian faith".

[
266
]

Both the Divisional Court (2:1) and the
Ontario Court of Appeal disagreed with the Commission’s argument.  Finlayson
J.A., writing for a unanimous court, held as follows at paragraph 48:

… it is my
opinion that actions taken pursuant to the Assembly's Standing Orders are
immune from examination by the Commission,
even when those actions are
alleged to breach the Code
. I consider it well established that the
Assembly must be afforded privilege over its own internal affairs and
day-to-day proceedings and that this privilege includes the setting of rules
such as the Standing Orders to provide for the proper functioning of the
Assembly. That is, matters relating to the internal workings of the House must
be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the House, since control over such
matters is necessary to the independent existence of the House. The House must
be absolutely free to set its own guidelines for how its legislative sessions
will be carried out and the Standing Orders that detail the operation of
parliamentary procedure must be considered privileged and insulated from
outside review. Having made this determination, it is not open to this court,
nor to any other body associated with the executive or judicial branches of
government, to question an individual exercise of conduct that falls within the
protected sphere. As the recitation of the prayers is called for by the
Standing Orders, it is encompassed as part of the Assembly's privilege relating
to control of its internal proceedings, and is not susceptible to outside
challenge. (Emphasis Added)

[
267
]

I acknowledge that
The Legislative Prayer
Case (Supra)
involved a statutorily created Commission and not a court.
However, I do not think that this makes a difference.  At paragraph 19
Finlayson J.A. stated:

The fact
that the Commission is a creation of the Legislature is of no significance in
this case. The Commission is simply an emanation of the Crown and is subject,
at the very least, to the same restrictions respecting the Legislature
as
are the judiciary
and the executive. (Emphasis Added)

[
268
]

Given that that the parliamentary
privilege in the case before me is necessary to the proper and dignified
functioning of the Legislature of Ontario, and that the reasons for which the
bans were issued fall within the privilege, I find that I do not have the
jurisdiction to review the actions of the Speaker in any manner, including under
the
Charter of Rights And Freedoms.

[
269
]

Given the findings that I made above, it
is not necessary to address the Applicants submissions that I should invoke the

Charter of Rights And Freedoms
to read down the
Trespass to Property
Act
so that it is consistent with
ss. 2 (b)
and (c) of the
Charter
,
or
that I stay the proceedings on the basis that they are an unjustifiable limitations
of their rights under these sections.

[
270
]

Also, all parties agree that since the
bans against all of the Defendants are now lifted, I do not have to adjudicate
on the issue of a declaration of invalidity of the bans as an unjustifiable
limitation of their rights under these sections, because it is a moot point.

[
271
]

Therefore, after having considered all of
the evidence, the relevant law and the submissions of the parties, based on the
above reasons, I find that the Crown proved the charges against all of the
Defendants beyond a reasonable doubt in that the evidence is uncontested that
on January 18, 1999 they entered the area from which they were banned.  They
are all found guilty as charged, of entering premises when entry prohibited, to
wit:  Queen’s Park on January 18, 1999.

[
272
]

Finally, the Defendants’ application for
costs is dismissed.
